blocks.x: Okay, that's where we're going. Let me start out with your name.
Albert Boyd.
Now, just where were you born?
Oh, right here in New Orleans.
Do you remember the street?
I was born in Priya and Allen. What was the date? March the 25th, 1902.
Were your parents musical? Did they play any instrument?
No. No, not that I know of. My father had a recording, but I don't think he ever played anything on it.
Any other relatives, uncles, or anybody else that ran city that played any instrument?
No.
How did you get interested in music when you were a boy? What's your very first memory of remembering hearing music, bands, or singing, or what it was?

Well, I had a brother who used to get a lot of picnics out of Millen Boyd. And Mount Perez. You know when Nelson used to play for him. Quite natural when they'd have things like that, they had to carry the children along. So, I'd be out there and listening at the music.
Yeah.
And, uh, well the only thing my mind was on is the clarinet. That's all I wanted to hear. Mm-hmm. And, uh, well at them time, most of the time, it would be Lovin Nelson that was playing.
Yeah. When you were a boy, what was your first instrument? When did you play on any, uh, even toy instruments, like kin flutes or anything else like some of them kids had?

No, I, uh, I tried fooling with harmonica, but that was too hard to fool with, and I was too hard to learn and figuring not to get anything out of it. Yeah. In those days, most everybody played harmonica. You never, boy, you don't own no record or anything. No. And, uh, well I wanted to clarinet, so the first chance I got, well I did buy a secondhand one. Mm-hmm. I bought a secondhand one from a fella.
How old were you? Do you remember him?
I was about seventeen.
From that? Mm-hmm.

Mm-hmm. And, uh, I bought one for nine dollars. And when I brought it home, I took it and started blowing on it. When I couldn't find out the mouthpiece had a piece missing out of it, and he had to fill it with wax. So I had to go buy a mouthpiece. I went and bought a mouthpiece. Yeah. And bought a mouthpiece. Well I kept that one a good while.
I was in the Albert system, no doubt. Oh yeah.
Yeah.
Did anybody have a banging system at all in those days that you knew?

Not that I know of, you know. Mm-hmm. And, um, well I took it and tried to practice on it. I didn't know what I was doing. So I tried to get Lorenzo Teo to teach me. I went to Lorenzo's house. He was staying on Seminar Street. I went to Lorenzo's house. And he agreed to teach me. He told me, he said, he told me to go buy a book. I told Angie and come to his house the following Wednesday.
Is that the young Lorenzo Teo? Yes.

Not the real old man? No, not the old man. So I went to his house that Wednesday with my book and here he comes to the door and I told him, well I care for my lesson. He said, well I'm sorry I can't give you any lessons. He said, because I'm leaving. I'm going to New York. Oh, that's bad.
It didn't happen. That was P-Roll. That's about it. So I left there.

Well, who could I try again? Well all the musicians was working. Pico and all those folks, they were working so much they didn't care to be bothered with teaching anybody. So I asked Pico, well he didn't have time to get on all this. The best thing I could do, well there was a fella that some fellas told me about, a fella by the name of Walter DeVoyne. He would play a little clarinet, you know. Well he was a tinsmith, so he was always willing to help somebody, you know. So I had a couple of fellas going to him. Well I went to him and he started me off.
Did you start with that same method then?

Yeah, with that same method. And he started me off. Well after I went to him for a while, for I'd say two, three months after I was gone to him. Well he learned me all he could. So I quit. Then by that time I lost practice, you know, my home trying to play numbers and I learned how to play a few numbers and I got to, I played a little job. A fella came and asked me to come play a job with him, just piano and clarinet. It was on a hollow night, I've forgotten what night it was. Just sort of party? Yeah, it was a house party. So a little galo it was.
Oh yeah.

So I went, I was wondering all the while, you know, I was going to make out. I had never practiced with a piano, with a nut. So I went there and we played the part where we made out alright. That was the first job I played.
Did you play everything by ear at that time or you had to do something? Oh yeah, yeah.
I was wondering what pieces of God would you play?
Did you play just the latest popular tunes or other waltzes or drag time or what kind of thing was it?
Oh at that time you had to play at that time, you had to play everything, you know, waltzes, people was dancing waltzes and a lot and... five shots and two steps and all.
Oh the latest tunes, I guess you knew those.
Yeah. At that time there was dancing waltzes a lot, you see. You had to mix them waltzes and you had to play two, three jump numbers and then waltzes. So we managed to make it.
Do you remember any of your other early jobs then, the very first ones after that?

Well, the first job I played with a band. I, Zeldon Morgan, was playing over at the Artesian Hall one night and the client up there, Adolfo was playing over at the Artesian Hall one night and the first one night was playing with him. For some reason he couldn't so he asked me to go over there. He sent me over there. That was my first job with a band. And well I, I was pretty fair there. Just playing by ear, you know.
Did the Morgan band, the Sam and Isaiah both, did they use music ever much or did they mostly just ear players?
Mostly, yeah. They, they, they, they'd get to, they'd get the music of a number and run over until they get it in the head and then put it aside.

Can you tell us some more about the very earliest musicians, especially the clarinet players that you heard, just what style they played, that is, if there was any difference in the style of Big Eye and say Piku or, of course I've heard both of them too, or the Teos. I never did get to hear any of the Teos. He was great. Lorenzo Junior, I guess. He was my favorite.
He was your favorite.
At that time, yeah.
Low and Lowitoo. Low was real good in them days.

There's one thing we were going to ask about, some of the musicians on clarinet will use, bite the top of the mouthpiece with the reed, I mean with the teeth, and others will cover the upper teeth with their lip. Did you ever do that?
I never bite the mouthpiece, I bite my lip.

You use the double embouchure, you would say, oh. Yeah. Your lip over both upper and lower teeth. Do you know which one of the old musicians did that? For instance, the Teos, do you know how they played Lorenzo Junior? Did he do that or bite on to it?

Well, I don't know, but I do believe this, that the majority of them bite their lip because I was told that that was the right way. There's only one man that I do know that used to bite the mouthpiece, and from playing the horn, from playing the horn a lot, his teeth cut a gutter in the mouthpiece, and that was George Abad.
I don't know. I never, it's hard to tell, you know, unless you're really a clarinetist and look at it, and so I never paid much attention to even Big Eye if he did that. Do you know how he?
No, I don't believe, because any man that do that in the long run, you'd see a gutter from their teeth, it wears down into the top of the mouthpiece.

Ralph here is taking lessons from Professor Mineta, and he advises him to do that too. He says some of the old timers that used to, I think he said George Bakay too, had his teeth all worn from, it wears not only the mouthpiece but the teeth. He said he used to go around and look at the clarinet fires, and quite a few of them would have their teeth worn down too there in the middle, and he didn't do that. And Sam Ducre taught him to use his lip on both upper and lower.
Well that's one thing I could take Waltz as a one for, he liked me. He taught me that.

And you still use that, you always did use that, at the very beginning. Barney Begard does it, and yet I've known other clarinetists that would bite onto the mouthpiece. I think George Lewis does that another day too. Yeah. Hello, come in, that's alright. We were just having a visit, talking here on the microphone here.
Well, just for curiosity, I tried that, because I knew the fellas was doing that, and I just tried that to see how it feels. I just couldn't stand it. No. The vibration.
Yeah, that's when it shakes your head and everything.
The vibration against your teeth acts on the bottom of the lawyer.
That's the way it did me. It did me. A little bit accurate. I couldn't see how they do it.
No. I never paid that much attention to how he left his horn, but I'm pretty sure he never, he never bite the mouthpiece with his teeth.

Did you hear any of his other folks, his uncle or father, Lorenzo or Papa, Teo, did you ever hear them play? Come on up there, Tony. Oh, I don't think I ever, I don't think I ever heard the old man play.

It was before your time, right? That was before my time, yeah. And had I, well, I don't remember when did he die, but I don't believe he was dead yet, you know, when I was trying to get somebody to teach me if I could do anything about him. Probably I'd have been able to get him.
Because Papa, Teo was a teacher quite a bit. Yeah, he had a lot of scholars. He taught some of those, Albert Nicholas too.
Yeah, I think he taught Bonnie Begard.
Yeah, I think Albert Nicholas, no, three or four. Even Big Eye Louie, I believe, took some lessons from Papa, Teo. Yeah. I think Big Eye taught him.
I took a few lessons from Big Eye Louie.
Well, you took some from him too. Yeah. I understand he never did use music so much, he had a wonderful ear. Did he teach you how to book though too, or just?

Yeah, well, yeah, he used the book. You see, after I left Walter Defining, well, you know, I went to Louie. Louie, there were some things that I had the wrong understanding about the division, and Louie straightened me out on that. And, well, I got out of work. I wasn't paying much, but I got out of work. So I thought, I said, well, Louie, I'm not coming for lessons right now because I'm not working. I won't be able to pay you. He said, well, that don't stop you from coming. I said, well, no, I don't want to be that way. So I just stopped going to him, you see. And when I went back to work, well, I still didn't go back there. So I got to playing around with little bands. And there was Bonnie Begard and Adolph Alexander. They was playing with a band by the name of Homer Begard. It was a trumpet player. You ever heard of him?
I knew of Emil Begard. That was Barney Sunko on violin.
No, this was a trumpet player, Homer Begard. I don't remember.
I've heard of him, but I don't remember.

Well, them guys just played with him. And, well, every time they get a job, they had a little more. They'd look for somebody to sit in their place. So a lot of the time they came and got me. Well, when I first stopped out, the fellas, when them fellas see me coming, they'd get angry. Because they couldn't play anything.
That was some kid that wasn't as experienced.

So, well, they kept sending me in their place. And I just kept practicing. And every time playing a number, I remember the key it was in. And I practiced hard for the next time. They'd send me an horn like that. So I got to play most of the numbers that they would play. So I'm a big guy, I saw him, Bernard, he told me, he said, listen, he said, you want to join my band? He said, if them fellas can send you in their place and you can make out on them jobs, he said, well, you can be in the band regular. I said, well, that's up to you. I said, well, all right. Now you're a member of the band. So I got to playing with them. I played with them a long time. And, well, he used to get a lot of work. And until I got something better, I'd forgotten.

Well, by the way, in regard to your teeth, did it ever wear your teeth at all through your lip? I guess it didn't. No. You never noticed any wear on your teeth then at all? Mm-mm. You still have your original teeth. I'm not trying to get personal or anything, but some people do play, George Lewis plays with false teeth in the helmet. Yeah. I think he said he's worn out one set of false teeth by just biting onto it. Yeah? I thought he'd bite them up, but I wasn't sure about it.
Yeah, he does. Yeah. Do you remember?
Oh. This way, it don't affect your teeth at all.
No.
That vibration through your whole head, I guess, on the teeth too, would be good for you.

I noticed it when I first started, the first few times I blew it, I didn't know about the lip. I just popped my teeth on it. And I noticed the shape, but I thought it was all right. Yeah. And when I went to Mineta, well, of course, he'd tell me differently.
Do you remember George Bakke? Did you hear him? He left here pretty early, I think, with Kepard and those fellows. Do you remember hearing him, though, when you were a boy? No, I don't.

The only time I seen George Bakke or knew anything of George Bakke, of course, I had heard of him. The only time I seen George Bakke was about a couple of years before he died. When he came back? Yeah, after he came back here, I seen him working up, rap off the street and the bar up.
Another player is Charlie McCurtis. Do you remember him? Charlie McCurtis?
Charlie McCurtis. I remember him, but I remember seeing him, you know, not hearing him much. Never heard him much. No.

Charlie McCurtis. What were the very first bands you heard when you were a boy, even parade bands and brass bands in the street? Do you remember any parades when you were real young, just a little kid, say maybe six or seven years old?
Well, when I was real young, I was a kid that didn't let go around the street. They kept me inside.
Yeah, a lot of children didn't.
And I was brought to play in my yard.
You told us where you were raised, what part of town was it, right around here was it?
Yes, that's not far from me, it's Semperm.
Yes. Which school did you go to, by the way? I usually forget to ask people where they went to school or anything about their childhood.

My first school was a private school, just about, just a block and a half from where I was living. Because after I was born and grew up big enough to go to school, we was living on the island between Johnson and Galvis. Was it one of the Catholic schools? Yes. That was the first school I went to, Miss Angelina Barnerys.
When was the first parade you ever saw that you can remember? Or anything like the Mardi Gras in those days, what they were like?
Oh, the Mardi Gras. Mardi Gras was something them days. That's better than now, I think.
Oh, so much better.
You had so many people with masks in those days. You had, in those days you had monkeys and so many bunch of guys which you had to get all messy. Red Devil and skeletons and all that.
Is there any special music around then, more than there is now on Mardi Gras? Well, no. Is there groups playing in the street, aside from the brass bands, anything special?

Well you'd have a lot of people would get a high band on the truck. Yeah, well I did. You had a lot of that. But the people would just mask those days in groups and just go around the street and have their fun and talking to people, calling people in the name that they know, they know that they didn't know who they was. Have them guessing. Have you ever played in any of those early Mardi Gras, Albert?
Or truck or anything?

No, but I'll tell you, when I first started to learn, I masked on the Mardi Gras. My sister was working at a factory and they asked me to mask with them and I masked with them and I took my clarinet and blowed that clarinet all day. In the street? Yeah, in the street and they was dancing behind me with tambourines. Yeah. And I was the only one playing anything.
The only one, no guitar or anything.
That was, and at that time, what's that, somebody's getting?

Yeah. I was wondering about the Indian dances those days. See, they still have the Indians in this part of town more around Galvez and Conti over in that section or even Claiborne. They sort of do this chanting and singing along with it. Do you remember any of those Indians in the old days? What the, the regular Indian clubs or whatever they call them? Well, I... Did that go way back when you were a boy? Do you remember?
Well, I remember the Pocahontas was one. Yeah.
Did they do any special dancing or music with it in those days? Any like drums or anything with them or?
No, they just go, go to the street dancing and put on Indian dance. Yeah. There was a bunch, there was a group used to meet at Bourbon, at, well it was Bourbon at that time but now it's Polga.
Oh yes.
Polga and Claiborne. Used to meet there.

I was gonna ask, you mentioned Alexander, is that Tatz, the young... That's Tatz. Because his father played in the brass bands too. Tatz, I understand uses, if I remember, uses the BAME system, clarinet now. Do you know if he started on that? I hadn't talked to him yet. In those days when you took his place, was he playing that or the...
I don't believe, I... I don't believe. I think he used to play the album system.

Probably changed then. Probably changed then. We'll ask him some of these days. I'll see him. I haven't talked to him yet. I don't think he had a tape. What was the first brass band you ever played in?
First brass band I played in, I think that was... I used to play on Carnival Day. That was a band, just got a job on Carnival Day.
So did you pick up from the make up band?
That was for the Jefferson City Buzzer, we used to play every year. That was with Tajama Garnier. He was a trumpet player. That was with Tajama Garnier.
He just got whoever he could find for that day, was that an organized band or was it?
Yeah, he had a regular group that he used to manage to get the same fellas every year. You know every year? Yeah, Booker T was playing drum, glass.
Booker T...
Henry Glass.
There's a drummer with that name up in Chicago, came from Memphis, I wondered if he really was. Booker T Washington, I know his name was.
Yeah, Booker T was playing drum and... I just can't think of the guy's name.
Any of the trombones, remember any of the trombones or...
I can't remember who was playing trombones.
Did they have any saxophones in those bands in those days or... Just the clarinet?
No, just clarinet.
They used alto horn or baritone, brass? Yeah. I'm wondering too about the E-flat clarinet, if you ever played that or ever had one or tried to play it? No, I never played the E-flat.
I had gotten one and it needed a pan and I took it and kind of fixed it up and blow it on it and I didn't like it. It's so high. Yeah. And I just put it down.
I never worried about playing O-E-flat. Did the fingering bother you any?
Was it being closer together or did that bother you? Just the... Oh yeah, a little. Because you have to get used to that close to finger.

And I never intended to play that much for red, you know. So I never worried about the E-flat. Do you remember some of the older Albert Sardin's band? Albert Sardin's band, if they had less keys than they have now, do you remember like the first one you got? Or some of the older players, the ones that you saw, if they had... how many keys did yours have?
About 13 is it or something? No. No. No. No. No. No. No. No.
No. Well, some of them had 13 keys.
Yeah.
13 and 15. I believe that was the last 13. Did any of them have less than that even on them? Not that I know of.
That would be with no rings on it, Albert Sardin's band?
No ring at the top. No ring at the top. I had a ring on the lower joint. Yeah.
I believe, I think I had one of them. I don't know.
I don't know. I don't know.
I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. I believe, I think I had one with no rings at all. I think Piku's got one ring. Yeah, I believe I had one with no rings at all.
What make is your tire net now?
That's La Casselle, the one I'm using now. French?
That's a French home.
Yes.
What kind do you prefer, if you had your choice? Is there any particular make like Buffet or Selmer or anything else that you'd like?
Well, I've been trying to locate a summer or a Buffet and I still would like to have one in Albert's system. Yeah, hard to find now.
But they are hard to find. Can you find any of any kind, Albert? Any? Well, yes.
They have a few in circulation. Sometimes you might run across one in a pawn shop. Yeah, yeah.
But it seems to be nearly all BAM now.
All BAM now. And in the music stores, they have some usements, you know. Oh, yes. The music stores they have.
Did you ever play the BAM at all to try it out to see how you'd like it?
No, I never tried.

I wondered if you knew if there's much difference in the tone or anything else. Just from hearing other people play them, do you think there's any difference in the tone? Some people think there's a difference and others say they can't tell much. I just wondered if you had any difference. Well, I believe there's a difference.
I believe there's a difference. I don't know what makes it, but I think there's a difference. It seems to me that they don't have as good a tone as the Albert system.

That's my impression too, but sometimes it may be because all the good players that I've known, just about all the good ones have used the Albert, so. I just wondered if you'd ever played both to see for yourself how you felt.
No, I never played any, but I listened to the fellas that played them, and the tone no sound is good as any one that plays an Albert.
What is the difference? How does it strike you? In what respect? Fuller, louder, prettier, in what way?
Well, louder, louder, and I don't know. I can't just explain it.

I know, that's hard to describe. I know that. I was wondering about your tone. You have not only a beautiful tone, but one of the good, full, big tones, which a lot of players, especially the younger players, now don't get a big tone. They're always covered up by the brass, the trumpet and trombone, which they can't cover you up. I wonder, how do you get that big tone? You don't look like you're blowing extra hard.
Is it something about peace? I think the main trouble is that they use too soft a reed.
How hard a reed do you use? I use three.
Three.
What kind of a mouthpiece do you use, Albert? Is it just a standard mouthpiece, or is it a con?
Well, the one I'm using now is a salmon.
Oh, a salmon mouthpiece. Would you say that was probably a little wider than the average?
Does it have a big lay? That is, did anybody ever file it down? I understand some of the New Orleans fellows used to file down that mouthpiece to open it up more between the reeds.

Well, that's the mistake they made, they ruined them. I have a couple of mouthpiece that that fellas ruined like that, that I got, and I couldn't blow them. A couple of mouthpiece that they ruined like that, file them down. Them mouthpiece comes by numbers. You can buy them open.
I've only seen the standard ones, they seem to be kind of...

I went, when I bought this one, I went to the store, and I was to get an H2S, but they gave me an H1S, which is not quite as wide open as the H2S. But after I had it a while, and I thought it was H2S, then I went, I happened to my Peterson to get something done on my phone. And he looked at it, and he said, well, he said, you were supposed to get H2S, it's H1S. But it was H2S that I was supposed to get. But you got used to it, you just as easy. I got used to it, yeah.
So dear to dear

I had a regular margillian or a cheap margillian, a big was an imperial. I paid two and a half for that margillian. And they kept telling me about the selmas, the selmas, the selmas. And that was the best margillian I ever had. No, that cheap margillian. And I bought this selma and I was taking it off my horn. I was playing at the Mardi Gras at the time. I had taken it off my horn and kept it in my case. Somebody swiped it out of my case. Somebody swiped it out of my case back there by the Mardi Gras.
Yeah, you wouldn't think anybody would have to... That's a load of steel. I'd steal more than that if we were going to steal something anyway.
It doesn't necessarily depend on the price of the mouthpiece. No. No. No.
Do you like it not too wide open then, you think? Or no? Does it make any difference in getting the big tone that you do to have it either wider or more narrow? What do you think?
Yes, it do. See, too close, when it's closed too much, when you blow hard, it'll close and nothing come out. It'll flop. That's right, yeah.
And if it's too wide, you have to blow so hard that you hardly have any wind left. Or too hard, yeah, you hardly have any wind left.
So you have to blow on them, you have to play, it'll take a while for you to find out exactly what you should have. That's right, yeah.

That's right, yeah. Now this one I'm using is the same as Mineta's mouthpiece, it's a Kahn. It's a Kahn? A Kahn mouthpiece. And I find it's a little wider than the average one, you know? Uh-huh. But I find that now I've got used to it, the other ones, they flop. Yeah.
Yeah. Got used to blowing hard. Well, you just, you just, I think you should try one of them H2S. I'd like to do that. What make is that? A Selmer.
Selmer.
On the Selmer.
I'd like to do that.
All the used to have, you could go, you could go right back to you, you know, on Brow Street.
Yeah.
Go there and try one.
Yeah. I'd like to do that. Would you say the H2S is a little better than the H1S that you've got?
It would be better for me, I think. Yeah. Of course, now that I got used to this one, I guess the problem would be about the same.
And you took up Clarenette, how much did you practice in the beginning when you first started?

Well, I practiced every chance that I got. And I was waking, I was waking at the daytime. I'd go to work at 7 o'clock in the morning and knock off at 5.30 in the evening. And I'd get up in the morning before I'd go to work and wake people in the neighborhood.
Be blowing on the clarinet.
And the time I'd come home in the evening, get something to eat, I'd go right back to it.

I'm wondering about some of the other bands you played with then after, oh, who was the first band? The big arts that you played with, you mentioned that you stayed with them a while. If you want to go on and tell about a few of the other bands.
Well, there's so many of them that I played with. We had a little band we made up. You remember, you heard of Johnny Deve?
Yes, they played the banjo with Sam Morgan, I know.
Yeah, well, we had a little band we made up. And I played with them a pretty good while.
Who was the carnette?
Henry Landry. He's away from here, I think he's in California. He put it down after, you know, after the band broke up.
Was he any relation to Big Landry, the big fella, the big guy, you know?
No, no relation.
How many were in that band? Do you remember the other players, like the trombone or bass?
There was six pieces. There were six pieces in that band. That's about the only ones I remember. Johnny Deve and Landry on trumpet.
Used trombone or any?
Yeah, they had trombone. I just can't remember who was playing the trombone. Or a bass player?
Bass.
Had a banjo. Yeah. Didn't have any sax, no? No. No sax. How long were you with them?
Very long or just a short time? Oh, I was with them a pretty good while. And I'd say for about a year. Then you remember your next band about that you went with?
Well, in fact, they was the first band I played with. Oh, that was before Omar. Yeah.

And I played with Omar Bernard a long time. And, uh, I played with Omar Bernard a long time. And, uh, I was with them a pretty good while. I'd say for about a year. Then you remember your next band about that you went with? Well, uh, in fact, they was the first band I played with. Then after I left them, I went with Omar Bernard.
Oh, that was after, that was before Omar. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. And I played with Omar Bernard a long time. And, uh, there was a trumpet player around here. I don't know if you ever heard of him. Bush Hall.
I've heard the name, yes.
He was a good little trumpet player. He played something on the order of Buddy Petit.
Mm-hmm.
He made a lot of chromatics. Well, I played with him several jobs, you know. Yeah.
For a while. Did you ever play with Buddy Petit? Oh, yeah.
I played with Buddy Petit. At the time I played with Buddy Petit, he had an eight-piece band. And he used to go out of town, all around Muggaloosa. Mm-hmm.
How many, you say, eight pieces that have two trumpets or sax? Oh, yeah.
I had a ten of sax. Henry Harden was playing tenor sax. Mm-hmm. And two trumpets.
Do you know about when that was? Say, would it be around 1925 or a little later or 19, early 1920s? Or any way to remember? Or how old you were when you played with Buddy? No, I don't.
But I think that should have been somewhere around between 25 and 30. Long in that period.
Long in that period.
Long in that period. Mm-hmm.
How was Buddy playing then? Oh, he was playing good.
Really good. Yeah.

Somebody told me once in his later days he didn't play as well as when he was real young. And I just wondered, that was near the end of his life then, wasn't it? Well, no. He played with him, I guess.
He might have not been quite as strong because he drank so hard. But he still was wonderful.
Well, he still was good.
Yeah. He had a different style from anyone I ever heard. His style was all together different.
What was he like? Did he play low or high or? He played low.
He played low.
He ever used mutes or just the open horn mostly or how? Yeah, he used mutes.
Mutes too.
Mostly the do-eby.
Those days, some fellas used the do-eby. All the things that you hear these fellas doing these mutes these days. Them fellas did all that just with the do-eby.
Would you find it would be easier to play with Albert if he was playing down low? You wouldn't have to keep getting over him all the time? Oh yeah, sure. So much easier to work. So much easier.
He played down low on the staff all the time. Wouldn't be getting in your way or something?
No.
No. There's nothing but a lot of chromatics.
Would he stick pretty well, you might say, to the melody so that you could… Yeah.
Oh yeah. Yeah.
Would you like coming down the brakes to sort of bridge it or would you be going over him all the time? How would you play with him? How would you do the do-eby?
Well, I'd just play my regular way, you know.

In those days, did the clarinetists play mostly in the upper register? Sometimes low register solos? Or how did they do it nowadays? They'd maybe take a whole chorus in the low register and then they'd take another chorus in the high? Yeah. How did you play in those days?

Well, I'd play my, I'd play, in those days I'd play my solos in the high register. I had a system, I had a system of my own that when I'd take solo, most of the time they'd let the clarinetists take two chords. Well, I'd play the melody, the first chords and then get off on the second. On the variations then?
Yeah. With the band, did you usually just play like chords and arpeggios up and down or other counter melody, more like another melody with it or more of the chords most of the time?
No, most of the chords. The chords, mm-hmm.

Did most of the clarinet players play that style or some of them maybe use more runs than others or are there many different styles on the clarinet or would you say most of the New Orleans fellas used about the same style?
It seems to me most of them played about the same style.
Some of the other players around I guess you got to hear, I think you mentioned George Boyd, did you once? Yeah, George Boyd.
What did he play like?
Because we never heard him, he died before he made any records and nobody, what kind of
a player was he?
Was he smooth or rough or did he, big tone or what was he?
He had a big tone. He was pretty strong, he had a big tone. He played, he was a kid punch clarinet.
Oh that's right, yeah. Did you ever play with punch too or any time?
Well I guess I only had the opportunity to play one job with him and that was an advertisement. On the truck. On the truck. Yes.
How was that kind of work, working on the truck Alba? Would that be harder than playing a dance or what would you say that kind of work would be?
No it wasn't harder than playing a dance because on the truck you'd just run, you'd just play about every second corner you'd play a short number. Just to draw the people's attention.
You'd usually play like a jump number or?
Yeah. Sometimes you'd play blues. Just mix them in you know.
Did you ever run into any other bands that way on the corners too?
Oh yeah, you'd run into a lot of bands. In those days yeah, meet up on the corners alongside each other. Made the best man win.
But you'd still keep playing short numbers. Oh yeah. About, what did you say, about two or four choruses?
About three or four choruses, yeah. Did you ever play with Chris? Everybody would pick their best numbers for advertising. Pick four or five numbers and just play that all the while they advertise.
Over and over again and he's called about the same ones. I started to ask if you ever played with Chris Kelly.
Well, Chris Kelly? I played one job with Chris Kelly.
How was he compared with, say, Punch or Buddy Petit and some of the other fellas?

Well, Chris was, Chris was a real, he was good. He was strong. But I'll tell you one thing. There was nobody, there was nobody to play a blues like Chris. He was a blues man. You couldn't get him to beat him playing the blues. Charlie Lewis will tell you that same thing because George played with him.
You mean all the variations and the things he'd do?
Yeah. The longer he'd play the blues, the better he'd play it. Oh yeah. Chorus after chorus? Chorus after chorus. He was really on blues.
Did he use the mute most of the time or just some of the time or how did he do that?
Just summertime.
Take one chorus with a mute and then one with Alice or something like that?
Yeah.
Them fellas really knew what to do with the derby.
Did you ever hear Louis Armstrong when he was young down here before he went north?
Not that I know of.

Or Joe Oliver? Anita. What would be the best of the old time bands that you ever heard that you can remember? If you had to pick one band either that you played with or that you didn't play with that you used to hear at dances. What would be the best band that you can think of that you've heard?
Well, for dancing I really did like Sam Morgan for dance music.
Did they have a better beat than the other bands or what made them good? The tempo or what was it that made them good?
Well, I just had a better beat.

How was Sam Morgan individually as a trumpet player? Was he one of the outstanding ones? That is, was he powerful and a wonderful tone or how was he compared to say Buddy Petit and Chris and the other fellows?
He was pretty strong and he had a real nice tone.
Did you ever play with Sam Morgan band? You mentioned Isaiah.
No, I never played with Sam.
Are there any of the other bands that you had notes about that you wanted to mention?
Well, I also played a short time with Bob Lyons.
Oh yeah, uptown then.
Yeah, played several jobs with him. And I played with the Olympia band which was Arnold Dupas. Drummer.
Who else was with the Olympia? Do you remember the trumpet player?
The trumpet player was Almer Talbot. Oh yeah.
How did he play in the old days? I heard him late years with George Lewis a couple of times. How did he play and was he real good early or how did he sound when...
He was about the same I think. About the same of it.
Yeah. Was he considered one of the better trumpet players? I never did know if he was considered one of the very best or just an ordinary one or what?
Just, well, I think he was just, he was considered just one of the ordinary ones. But, but he was, he was such a good showman with his singing, you know.
Well, I started to ask about Emmanuel Perez. I no doubt you heard him. He stayed down here all his life.
Yeah, well I, I played a couple of jobs with Emmanuel Perez. I did Millen Boy. A couple of times I played out there with him.
I was going to ask about the, when you played with Bob Lyons. Can you remember anybody who was in the band then, at that time?
The only one I can remember was Rudolph, Rudolph Boyle.
Yeah, what did he play?
The drummer.
Oh, the drummer.
Big, big guy. Ever said that fella? Tall, ever said.
Yeah. Where did you play with Bob Lyons? Is it dances or private parties or homes or what?
We played several parties. I don't think I played about four or five times with that group.

In regard to Emmanuel Perez, you say you played out at Millenburg? Yeah. How late did they have those camps out at Millenburg? Do you remember about how they were? Do you remember about how late you played with Emmanuel and when they tore it down out there?
Oh, I can't remember yet.

Well, the other people in his band at that time, Trombone, who he used. Everyone else. I know it's difficult when you only played maybe a couple of nights. Yeah. The person remembers us who was there 20 or 30 years ago.
The only one I can remember in his line was this Sam drummer. Glass, Henry Glass. That's the only fella I remember that was on that job. How did Perez play?
He's another one I never had the chance to hear him play. How was he? Oh, he was powerful.
He was powerful.
Yeah, powerful.
Yeah, he was powerful.
Did he have a big range, high notes and low too, or how did he do in that respect?
He didn't go very high, but he was so powerful. Did you ever play with him? He put such force behind it that you'd think it was a high note.
Oh, yeah. Did you play with him how much? Very often? You think he played at Millen.
No, I only played two or three jobs with him at that same place that was on Sunday night or Saturday. I did three or four times with him.
What I was wondering was if he was easy to work with.

I mean, would you say there was any particular kind of trumpet player that is easier to work with, like a man that stays and plays in the staff most of the time? Would you say it would be easier to play a clarinet with?
Well, yeah. A man that stays and is deaf and also a man that sticks to his melody. That makes it easier for the clarinet.
In other words, you say a man like some of these instruments play nowadays, they play all those high notes and that kind of bop stuff. You'd say that would be hard for a clarinet to play? Well, sure.
Yeah. I know it's hard for me. It's hard for you.
It's hard for you.

It's hard for you. Now, if you have your list there, any other jobs then after those that you mentioned, Bob Lyons and the, is it Darmul Dupass or somebody that you played for at? Right. Right. And who some of your later bands were in the recent years?

Well, I played with Willie Paggio. We played up on, at Burgundy and Canelo, there was a jet and dance upstairs. And I played up there with Willie Paggio for about a year. But before that we played as the Charles and Padres for about six months. Was that another? Another Jitney dance.
Jitney dance. And Willie Meenbart was playing piano. Oh yes.
Ellie Biggaard was playing trombone.
Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. And Willie Meenbart was playing piano.
Oh yes. Ellie Biggaard was playing trombone. Mm-hmm. Yang Johnson was playing trombone.
When did Yang die about, do you know? I never knew him or his brother.
Did he live longer than Buddy Johnson? Oh yeah. Yeah.
Buddy was dead a good while before him.
Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
with Willie Paggio. Who did you go with? Do you remember?

Well, I used to get a lot of weight myself, and I used to get a little line up, you know? Sure. I had a line up, a four-piece line up. I had myself, Albert Tablin on trumpet, Albert Giles on drums, and Clannis Gabriel on piano, four pieces. We used to play at the Dandy Inn. That was on Jefferson Davis.
I heard you out there. You did? 1938, about.
Yeah.
I know a little bit later in that. It was later in that.
Oh, he went out there a good while until he got ready to close down. Then after that, well, after that, there was trios was taking things over, you know? Yeah. Yeah. Had a lot of weight for trails.
I used to hear you out on Magazine Street one time with a trio too, a guitar.

Yeah, well, I got a three-piece lined up of my own. I had, I called it the three Ls. It was, I was playing piano then, Albert Giles playing drums, and I had Al, Al, playing ghetto. I guess that's the one I heard.
You worked with Johnny St. Sarah then later too, didn't you, for a while?

I worked around, well, I worked, yeah, I worked around, on Decatur Street, they had a lot of joints on Decatur Street, before Budapest Street got popped in. I played around there with a lot of three and four-piece bands. I played around there with Johnny St. Sarah too. Johnny St. Sarah played with me an old Lego band one time.
When did you join Bill Matthews? How long has that been now?
Well, a rough guess, I think it's about five years.
How long? I couldn't remember.
Because I was with Paul Barberin.
Yes, that's right.

At the time, I was with Paul Barberin, and, well, they asked me, they offered me the job. I threw it down the first time. You could have it. Well, the next time, I came from Paul Barberin and do nothing much, so I just accepted it. And I've been with them ever since.

How do you like that kind of work, Alba? Well, it's all right. I mean, what do you think of the kind of music? I mean, I notice you hardly ever play blues. It's all pretty well, I must say, jump numbers. Yes. Do you find that kind of hard work?
Well, it is kind of hard, because it would be a little easier if you play a couple of fast ones and a slow one.

They make you play the saints almost every set, I guess. Almost every set. You do that marching around the place. I guess the tourists like it all right. Were there some other bands in there, any other notes that you had there that you wanted to go over? We're just about through with that tape here. We don't want to bother you so much about every little detail, but I thought if there were some other bands you might have left out, any other notes on the paper that you wanted to mention before we...
Well, there's only one thing I'd like to mention concerning the fellas that I've taken lessons from.
Oh, yeah.
The last fella that I've taken a few lessons from was Lionel Dupal. You ever heard of him?
I don't know him at all. I've heard of him. He don't play anymore,
but he was a good musician.
Is he still here? He's the one
that taught Henry Julian. You ever heard of Henry Julian?
No.

Well, that was Henry Julian's grandfather. He was a saxophone player with the Olympic Band. And when I joined the Olympic Band, well, he got me to go to his grandfather for lessons. Lionel Dupal had not taken lessons, a few lessons with him.
Is he still around? Living?
Yeah. He's living. He's a bricklayer, I think. He's a plasterer or a bricklayer.
Do you have his address? We'd like to talk to him sometime, too, you know?
Well, I may be able to get it out the phone book. It's in the phone book. You think it's in the phone book? Yeah, it should be.
Well, look it up there.
D, yeah. If you don't mind, I'll get it for you before you leave.
Yes. How do you spell the last name?
I think it's D-U-P-E-A-U-D. That's why I tell you, he best let me look for you. Yes.

Yes. Those French names, three old names. You're right. Is there anything else there that you wanted to say before we quit on this about either any of the old-time musicians that you admired and who was your favourite if you had to, I don't like to put you on the spot, but if you had to pick one clarinetist, the greatest you ever heard, who would be your one favourite?
Well, that's pretty hard to tell because there's two, three of them that I
Well, then who are the two of the three?
And I think Johnny Dyes.
Did you ever get to hear
Jimmy Noon? Jimmy Noon, Johnny Dyes, Lorenzo Teo, that's my favourite.
Those three?
And Big Island, too.
Yes, he was fine.
Did you ever hear either Johnny Dodds or Jimmy Noon down here and all?
No, that's just what I was about to say. I never heard them in poison, but they're reckons. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
I knew them both in Chicago, not so well, but I'd hear them four or five times in person in my life and they were both wonderful. But I didn't get to hear Tee on. I regret it.
You didn't get to hear him. He was great. Such wonderful tone and so clean.
Everything clean. Is he a good improviser? Could he fake as well as anybody else, too?
Oh, yes.
Yes, indeed.
Did you ever get to hear a George Barquet tone? He said no. No, no, no, no.

Did Tee O play much in the low register? He made a few records, of course, on with P-Rone and they're not too well recorded and you can't hear the clarinet too well just what he's doing. Some of them sound like they were all written out in arrangements, too, but I wondered if he was a good, as they say, a good hop player, too, that could improvise well and all of that. Is he?
Yeah, I think so.
Mm-hmm. He'd be way up high.
He played so clean. Mm-hmm. He played so clean. And he said clean, like each note would be cut cut off. Yeah, you know, no fumble. Yeah. I wish I'd heard him.
Oh, Albert, did you ever try a plastic reed? Did you ever try it? Did you ever try it?
Yeah, I tried.
I tried. I tried. I tried. I couldn't get anything to play, as long as I had
to play, as long as I had to play, as long as I had to play, as long as I had
to play, as long as I had to play, as long as I had to play, as long as I had to play, as long as I had to play, as long as I had
to play, as long as I had to play, to play,

to play, I couldn't get anything out of it. As long as I'd play, as long as I'd finger low, it'd be alright. When I'd try to make a high note, it would close on me. And I was told from someone that used the plastic reed, that after you get used to the plastic reed, you wouldn't be able to use the wooden reeds, the cane reeds, you know, after you get used to the plastic reed. So I decided not to fool with it, because I don't believe you could get a tone out of a plastic reed like you get out of a cane reed, for this reason, they don't get moisted.
It doesn't soak into them, I said.

No. You take a clarinet reed, you take a cane reed, most of the time you have to soak it in water by five minutes, to put it on your home, for it to blow right. But those things, they, those plastic reeds, you can't do anything with them.
Is that what you do with your reeds, Albert? You mean before you blow them, before you first get them? Yeah.
Each night when you go to play, do you just sort of wet it with your tongue a little bit, or do you try to soak it a little bit there too?

I wear it with my tongue, you see. Sometime you can take a reed out of the box and slap it on your horn, and it'll, and it'll suit you just right. Well, in that case you just use it. But sometime it'll, when you blow it, it'll feel like it's a little too stiff or something. Well, you take it, and you soak it for about five or ten minutes in water.
So it'll soften up a little bit. Yeah. I was going to say, do you...
Because it do make a difference after you soak that water.

It must soften it a little bit. It do. I was going to say, do you have your reed level with the end of your mouthpiece, a little bit down, a little bit up? No, a little bit down. A little bit down. Yeah. Do you find that protects the reed a little bit? It do.

Yeah, it protects the reed because sometimes, because your will hit it with your tongue, and by being below that, it protects the reed and it makes your horn, and it gives you a better tone. Yeah. Mm-hmm.
Yeah. I guess that... Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

segments.title: Birth in 1902, non-musical family and hearing clarinet at picnics
segments.summary: His parents and relatives did not play; he heard bands at picnics and wanted only to hear the clarinet.

segments.title: Buying his first secondhand clarinet
segments.summary: After trying harmonica, he buys a used clarinet at about seventeen for nine dollars and needs a new mouthpiece.

segments.title: Seeking lessons from Tio and Walter DeVoyne; first job
segments.summary: Lorenzo Tio is leaving for New York, so he studies with Walter DeVoyne and then plays his first house-party job with a piano.

segments.title: Repertoire at early dance jobs
segments.summary: He played by ear and had to mix waltzes and jump numbers at dances.

segments.title: First band job at Artesian Hall with the Morgans
segments.summary: He is sent to substitute at Artesian Hall for the Morgan band, his first band job; the Morgans were mostly ear players.

segments.title: Old clarinetists and biting the mouthpiece versus lip embouchure
segments.summary: Discussion of the Tios, Big Eye and others, and whether to bite the mouthpiece or cover the teeth with the lip; Burbank uses the lip.

segments.title: Papa Tio and Lorenzo Tio as teachers; lessons from Big Eye Louis
segments.summary: The interviewers talk about Papa Tio's pupils; Burbank took a few lessons from Big Eye Louis Nelson.

segments.title: Subbing for Begard and Alexander and joining Bernard's band
segments.summary: After stopping lessons, he subs for clarinetists in Homer Begard's group and is invited into Bernard's band as a regular.

segments.title: Teeth wear and clarinet playing
segments.summary: They compare dental wear from biting the mouthpiece, including George Lewis's false teeth.

segments.title: George Baquet and Charlie McCurtis
segments.summary: Burbank saw Baquet only briefly after his return and remembers McCurtis by sight.

segments.chapter: Childhood, Mardi Gras and first brass band
segments.title: Childhood neighborhood and first school
segments.summary: Raised indoors near Semperm, he attended a private Catholic school.

segments.chapter: Childhood, Mardi Gras and first brass band
segments.title: Mardi Gras in his youth and masking with a clarinet
segments.summary: He recalls masked groups, and once masked and played clarinet in the street.

segments.chapter: Childhood, Mardi Gras and first brass band
segments.title: Mardi Gras Indians in the old days
segments.summary: He remembers the Pocahontas Indians dancing in the street and meeting at Claiborne.

segments.chapter: Childhood, Mardi Gras and first brass band
segments.title: Tats Alexander's clarinet system
segments.summary: Burbank thinks Alexander played the Albert system back then.

segments.chapter: Childhood, Mardi Gras and first brass band
segments.title: First brass band: Tajama Garnier's Carnival Day band
segments.summary: He played Carnival Day each year in Garnier's brass band with Henry Glass on drums, clarinet only and no saxophones.

segments.title: E-flat clarinet and number of keys on old clarinets
segments.summary: He tried an E-flat clarinet and disliked it; they discuss key counts and rings on older Albert system clarinets.

segments.title: Albert system versus Boehm and his current clarinet
segments.summary: He plays a French clarinet, prefers the Albert system and thinks the Boehm tone is less good.

segments.title: Getting a big tone and reed strength
segments.summary: He says players use too soft a reed; he uses a number three.

segments.title: Mouthpieces: filing, H1S versus H2S and a stolen mouthpiece
segments.summary: Filed-down mouthpieces are ruined; he describes his H1S and a stolen Selmer mouthpiece.

segments.title: How mouthpiece opening affects blowing
segments.summary: Too closed a facing flops, too open wastes wind; they discuss trying an H2S.

segments.title: Practicing in the beginning
segments.summary: He practiced before and after his day job, waking the neighbors.

segments.title: Early small band with Johnny Deve and Henry Landry
segments.summary: His first band was a six-piece group with Deve and Landry, lasting about a year.

segments.title: Playing with Omar Bernard and trumpeter Bush Hall
segments.summary: He played a long time with Bernard and several jobs with Bush Hall, who played like Buddy Petit.

segments.title: Playing with Buddy Petit and his style
segments.summary: Burbank recalls Petit's eight-piece band, out-of-town jobs, low-register melodic style and use of mutes, and how a clarinet fits with it.

segments.title: Clarinet solo style in the old days
segments.summary: He took high-register solos and played chords behind the band; he thinks most New Orleans clarinetists played alike.

segments.title: Clarinetist George Baquet's tone and a job with Punch Miller
segments.summary: He describes a big-toned clarinetist and plays one advertising job with Punch.

segments.title: Truck advertising jobs and band battles on corners
segments.summary: Playing short numbers from a truck and meeting rival bands at corners.

segments.title: Chris Kelly as a blues trumpeter
segments.summary: He played one job with Kelly and praises his blues playing and mute work.

segments.title: Best old bands: Sam Morgan for dancing
segments.summary: He never heard young Armstrong or Oliver in New Orleans; Sam Morgan's band had the best beat for dancing.

segments.title: Bob Lyons, the Olympia band and Almer Talbert
segments.summary: He played short stints with Bob Lyons and Arnold DePass's Olympia band, and recalls Talbert and Rudolph Boyle.

segments.title: Emmanuel Perez and the Milneburg camp jobs
segments.summary: He played a few weekend jobs with Perez, who was powerful rather than high.

segments.title: What trumpet players are easiest for a clarinetist
segments.summary: A trumpeter who sticks to the melody is easier to play with than one who plays high bop-style notes.

segments.title: Willie Paggio and the jitney dance on Burgundy
segments.summary: He played about a year with Paggio at an upstairs dance, with Willie Meenbart on piano and trombonists.

segments.title: Leading his own small groups and Decatur Street joints
segments.summary: He led a four-piece at the Dandy Inn, a trio, and played with Johnny St. Cyr around Decatur Street.

segments.title: Joining Bill Matthews' band after Paul Barbarin
segments.summary: He took the Matthews job about five years earlier, playing mostly jump numbers and the Saints.

segments.title: Lessons from Lionel Dupeaud, Henry Julian's teacher
segments.summary: He last took lessons from Dupeaud, and promises to find his address.

segments.title: Favorite clarinetists: Noone, Dodds, Tio and Big Eye
segments.summary: He names Jimmy Noone, Johnny Dodds, Lorenzo Tio and Big Eye as favorites and praises Tio's clean playing.

segments.title: Plastic reeds and soaking cane reeds
segments.summary: He rejects plastic reeds and explains how he wets reeds and sets them slightly below the tip.
